item.title: How Latin America’s rightwing politicians use humour to normalise their extremist ideologies
item.description: Their jokes undermine public trust in institutions, encourage reactionary movements and weaken social cohesion by fostering division.
item.content:encoded:
Humour plays a key role in the political communication of rightwing populist leaders in Latin America. Politicians including Javier Milei in Argentina, Nayib Bukele in El Salvador and Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil have all used humour to engage with and solidify their support base, normalise extreme ideologies and deflect criticism.

Humour also circulates constantly among their followers. In October 2022, a few months before Brazilians went to the polls in their last general election, I carried out fieldwork at a Bolsonaro rally in the Brazilian city of Rio de Janeiro with a group of colleagues.

We overheard a Bolsonaro supporter joking about a stray dog. “Watch out for that dog!” he shouted. “If Lula wins, we’ll have to call him picanha [a type of beef].”

The crowd laughed, with another supporter adding: “If Lula wins, he’ll be the first to eat it.” Lula went on to be elected as Brazil’s president by a razor-thin margin.

Argentina held elections the following year to appoint successors to President Alberto Fernández and his vice-president, Cristina Fernández de Kirchner – who had dominated Argentinian politics for two decades alongside her husband, Néstor Kirchner. Together, they had forged Kirchnerism, the country’s main leftwing populist movement.

item.title: Bill criminalising insults to ‘Vande Mataram’ passed in Rajya Sabha
item.description: The bill states that preventing the singing of the national song can be punished with imprisonment of up to three years or a fine or both.
item.content:encoded:
The Rajya Sabha on Wednesday passed a bill criminalising insults to the national song, Vande Mataram.

The 2026 Prevention of Insults to National Honour Amendment Bill was passed in the Upper House by voice vote as the Opposition protested and shouted slogans demanding a response from Union Home Minister Amit Shah over the police action against protesters seeking educational reforms last week.

#MonsoonSession

Rajya Sabha passes The Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026.@nityanandraibjp @AmitShah @HMOIndia pic.twitter.com/lD7qstyY05

— SansadTV (@sansad_tv) July 29, 2026

The bill, which was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on Friday, seeks to accord Vande Mataram the same statutory protection as the national anthem, Jana Gana Mana. It states that intentionally preventing the singing of the national song, or causing disturbance to an assembly singing it can be punished with imprisonment of up to three years, a fine or both.

At present, the 1971 Act provides that insulting the national anthem, Jana Gana Mana, the national flag or the Constitution is punishable with up to three years’ imprisonment, a fine or both.

During a discussion on the amendment on Wednesday, Union Minister of State for Home Affairs Nityanand Rai accused the Congress of insulting Vande Mataram by resorting to appeasement politics, PTI reported.

item.title: Reservoir for Chennai could dry up ecologically-rich coastal wetland
item.description: The Great Salt Lake has long functioned as a fishing ground, a seasonal habitat and a flood buffer.
item.content:encoded:
Narayanan R stood on the muddy bund of the Great Salt Lake, watching a group of flamingoes pick their way across the shallows. He remembered standing in the same spot as a 10-year-old, knee-deep in water – the day his father showed him how to fish. “The flamingoes may not come next season,” he said. “These pools will dry soon.

A few hundred metres away, Gowriamma waded through the shallow waters of the lake, her fingers sifting through the mud for shrimp. “Everything depends on these small pools. We know this water through the mud and the thorns.”

Located between Nemmeli and Kovalam in Chennai, the Great Salt Lake also known as Kovalam-Nemmeli backwaters, is a coastal wetland that spans 5,000 acres. The Tamil Nadu government plans to convert this coastal wetland into Chennai’s sixth drinking water reservoir: the Mamallan reservoir.

Chennai currently supplies between 700 and 800 million litres per day of water. The demand already exceeds 1,100 MLD and is projected to cross 2,500 MLD by 2035, according to the project’s environmental impact assessment. item.title: Booker Prize 2026: A reader’s guide to the 13 novels (including two by past winners) on the longlist
item.description: The shortlist will be announced on September 22 and the winner on November 9. The winning author will get a cash prize of £50,000.
item.content:encoded:
The Booker Prize announced its 2025 longlist of thirteen titles on Tuesday. The longlisted authors represent seven countries and three continents. Past winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart and previously shortlisted author Elizabeth Strout are on this year’s longlist, alongside ten authors who are longlisted for the first time – including three debut novelists.

Should either James or Stuart win this year, they’ll join an elite list of four authors who have won the Booker Prize twice: JM Coetzee (1983 and 1999), Peter Carey (1988 and 2001), Hilary Mantel (2009 and 2012) and Margaret Atwood (2000 and 2019).

The shortlist will be announced on September 22, and the winner, on November 9. The winner will receive £50,000, while the shortlisted authors will each receive £2,500.

This year’s jury is chaired by writer Mary Beard, and she’s joined by writer and educator Raymond Antrobus; musician, writer and broadcaster Jarvis Cocker; journalist, editor and critic Rebecca Liu; and Booker Prize-shortlisted novelist Patricia Lockwood.

Announcing the longlist, Beard said, “Great books have never been written to a single formula. We are confident that our longlist of books has something for everyone. There’s the funny and the unsettling (and in some cases the funny and unsettling); there’s dystopian fantasy and domestic drama;...

item.title: Bill to amend anti-paper leak law passed in Lok Sabha after nationwide protests
item.description: The legislation was passed amid slogans by the Opposition MPs, demanding ‘justice’ for the students who took part in the march to Parliament on July 20.
item.content:encoded:
The Lok Sabha on Wednesday passed a bill to amend the anti-paper leak law through a voice vote.

The bill will now be moved to the Rajya Sabha. If cleared by the Upper House of Parliament, it will be sent for presidential assent.

The 2026 Public Examinations Prevention of Unfair Means Amendment Bill was introduced by Union minister Jitendra Singh on Monday, days after nationwide protests against alleged irregularities in the conduct of competitive examinations.

The legislation proposes imprisonment of five to ten years for individuals found using unfair means in public examinations. The maximum fine for such persons would increase from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 50 lakh.

Speaking in the Lok Sabha, Singh said that the government took swift action in the 2026 National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test paper leak case. He added that 52 first information reports had been lodged since the 2024 Public Examinations Prevention of Unfair Means Act came into force.

The bill was passed amid slogans by the Opposition MPs, demanding “justice” for the students who took part in the march to Parliament on July 20. Dozens were injured as the police used lathis, fired tear gas shells and pellet guns against the demonstrators.

item.content:encoded:
Chief Monk Lobsang leaves the Sarnai Monastery at twilight sans parting ceremony or retinue. It isn’t a joyous occasion to require as much. Climbing down the ancient, worn-out ladder that connected the Sarnai Monastery to Mang Yul strains his old bones, but he carries on.

He chooses to not traverse through the deadwood of the Baika Forest, but rather skirt around it, evading the shrine of the tutelary deities of the forest – 30 smooth stones smeared with red ochre and cordoned off with ropes – heading for the small pastoral village of Bayarma, south of the capital. The new capital, Lobsang corrects himself.

item.description: A bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant allowed Singh’s appeal challenging the summons issued to him by a trial court in 2015.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday accepted the Central Bureau of Investigation’s decision to close the case against former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh in an alleged coal allocation scam, Bar and Bench reported.

A bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant allowed Singh’s appeal challenging the summons issued to him by a trial court in 2015.

The order came a year-and-a-half after the former prime minister died in December 2024.

On Wednesday, advocate Kapil Sibal told the court that while Singh’s appeal may have technically become infructuous, or no longer relevant, after his death, the trial court’s adverse observations against the former prime minister required judicial interference, Live Law reported. Sibal urged the court to expunge those observations.

The Supreme Court remarked that although Singh’s death meant that the appeal could be disposed of as infructuous, it was important to look into whether the trial court’s decision to summon him was legally valid.

item.title: Slow trial violates right to liberty: SC grants bail to two UAPA suspects after 12 years in custody

item.content:encoded:

A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta held that the continued incarceration of the suspects amounted to a violation of their fundamental right to personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution.

The court has directed the release on bail of Mohammed Saquib Ansari and Waqar Azhar, subject to conditions imposed by the trial court and provided they were not required in any other case, the legal news outlet reported.

Justice Madhav Jamdar added that citizens are entitled to hold different opinions and quashed externment orders banning two members of the Social Democratic Party of India from entering Mumbai for a period of one year.

item.description: An excerpt from ‘What Happened to Me? vs What’s Wrong with Me?’, by Gunjan Y Trivedi, Riri G Trivedi, and Hemalatha Ramani.
item.content:encoded:
Growing up in a home with parental mental illness, suicide attempts, domestic violence or addiction increases the risk of long-term mental health and behavioural issues in children when they grow up. They may face emotional neglect, physical abuse andlong-lasting struggles with trust, self-esteem and mental health.


Pallavi, 24, came to us with severe depression, an eating disorder and intense anger. In rage, she would bang her head or hit herself.

“There is nobody for me in this world,” she said quietly.

She also struggled with compulsive needs around bathrooms and cleanliness, something she felt too ashamed to tell anyone. Even though she was an only child, she felt emotionally distant, almost disconnected, from both parents.

item.title: Assam flood toll rises to 75
item.description: Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma increased the ex gratia payment for the families of those killed in the floods to Rs 9 lakh from Rs 4 lakh.
item.content:encoded:
The toll in flood-related incidents in Assam rose to 75 on Tuesday after seven more deaths were reported in Sivasagar district, the state disaster management authority said.

Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma on Tuesday announced that the ex gratia payment for the families of those killed in the floods had been increased to Rs 9 lakh from Rs 4 lakh. An additional Rs 5 lakh will be provided from the Chief Minister’s Relief Fund.

Sarma also said that families would not need to submit a post-mortem report to claim the compensation, PTI reported. Instead, a certificate issued by the circle officer concerned would suffice, the chief minister added.

In cases where a person remains missing and the body is not recovered within a month, the government will provide Rs 9 lakh in ex gratia assistance to the family.

Charaideo was the worst-affected district, with 1.4 lakh persons affected, followed by Sivasagar with 97,074 and Jorhat with 57,371.

About 45,342 hectares of cropland has been submerged, while 622 villages continued to be affected by the floods.

The Dhansiri river continues to flow above the danger level in Numaligarh district, the authorities said.

A total of 81 relief camps are currently operational, sheltering 32,477 displaced people. Additionally, 34 relief distribution centres are functioning across the affected areas.

item.title: What erotic nutcuters reveal about the sensual history of paan in India
item.description: Antique sarotas fashioned as embracing couples reveal how betel chewing was once intertwined with courtly love, status and aesthetic pleasure.
item.content:encoded:
If you’ve ever wondered how Indians set the mood in centuries past, one potential answer is: cutting nuts – the areca kind.

That possibility is suggested by the existence of highly suggestive nutcutters preserved among exhibitions of antique domestic objects. A prime example is the display at the Raja Dinkar Kelkar Museum in Pune, arguably India’s largest collection of everyday artefacts from the early to late modern period in western and southern India. Housed since the 1960s in a traditional Puneri wada in one of the city’s old peth neighbourhoods, the museum’s curation of nutcutters – called adkitta in Marathi, sudi in Gujarati and sarota in Hindi – is especially noteworthy for its size, diversity and craftsmanship.

Alongside more respectable versions bearing animal and bird motifs or plain geometric designs sits a curious collection of erotic nutcutters. Made of brass and silver in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Rajasthan during the 18th and 19th centuries, these objects depict couples in a variety of amorous poses. Yet the Kelkar Museum’s risqué sarotas are not merely titillating curiosities but represent a pedigreed lineage of erotic imagery intertwined with the consumption of areca nuts as part of the sophisticated cultural practice of betel chewing.

Between November 2026 and June 2027, rice will be sold to ethanol distilleries for Rs 2,390 per quintal, it added.

The public sector organisation dispatched 6.3 million tonnes of rice worth Rs 14,596 crore to ethanol producers during the 12-month period.

item.title: The Emergency’s ghost: Why India has been placed on the watchlist of a global civil society network
item.description: A key factor in including India on the Civicus watchlist is the continued judicial persecution of human rights defenders and protest leaders.
item.content:encoded:
Fifty years ago, India was in the midst of the Emergency. Prime Minister Indira Gandhi’s government had suspended civil liberties, censored the press and imprisoned tens of thousands of protesters.

Today, there is no formal declaration of emergency or suspension of fundamental rights under the constitution. But the parallels are hard to miss.

As we write this, a nationwide protest movement triggered by young people frustrated at the denial of their voices and the lack of opportunities has been met with brutal police action. A film about a human rights defender slain 30 years ago has inexplicably been taken off the streaming platform that had hosted it.

Provisions of the Foreign Contributions Regulation Act, introduced in 1976 during the Emergency, have been amended again to further tighten the state’s grip on civil society organisations that work to uncover high-level corruption, environmental degradation and human rights violations.

As during the Emergency, the state’s investigative agencies have been weaponised to go after dissidents, using the time-tested bogey of national security and fear of foreign influence to silence those not aligned with the ruling party.

item.title: ‘I see you in my sleep / Awake, you are an absence I endure’: A poem for vanishing sparrows
item.description: Mukul Kesavan’s poem for World Nature Conservation Day.
item.content:encoded:
Note to a Sparrow

In childhood, chasing chidiyas round a room
was sport. Exhausted, you would fall and flutter.
I’d switch the fan off first to ward off doom;
I was a wanton boy… not a nutter.
We didn’t have a proper word for sparrow,
You were generic birds who lived at home,
Like dogs and sibs, but not as pets or kin,
Free to flit past Amma’s straight-and-narrow,
To feed and nest and roam,
To fly, while grounded mammals mooched within.

I haven’t raced you now in sixty years,
My children have no memories of you,
In times deranged by grand extinction fears
I wonder what the two of you will do.
I see your painted head and inky bib,
The twitchy way you tilt your head and cheep,
I see her face, pale eyebrowed and demure,
Your wife for life, this hot and flighty rib.
I see you in my sleep;
Awake, you are an absence I endure.

An absent sparrow is an awful thing,
An order of the ordinary gone,
The nightingale forgetting how to sing
Is not the same, the world will carry on.
I want you back inside my balcony
Astir within your made-to-measure nest,
Intent on kissing up a brood of you.
I’ll find an icon of Saint Anthony
To guard your sated rest,
You’ll be a sign the world is back in true.

Or not. Two fostered sparrows won’t repair
A broken world or douse the hidden fire
That fogs your balcony with charry air
And folds the earth into a poisoned gyre.
And yet, to share a common wall with you
To live adjacently...

item.title: Interview: What Lakshadweep can teach the rest of India about eliminating TB
item.description: Localised care and working closely with communities was crucial to the archipelago eliminating TB by March 2021.
item.content:encoded:
Lakshadweep is India’s smallest Union Territory, an archipelago consisting of 36 islands – 10 of which are inhabited – with an area of 32 sq km. But most islands are two to five hours away on choppy seas, and one particular island, Minicoy, takes a 16-hour ship journey from the headquarters, Kavaratti.

It is in this archipelago that India found its first success on TB elimination. Lakshadweep was declared TB-free in March 2021, three years after a strategy document spelt out the task ahead of the administration.

“The strategy was simple in the way many great public health ideas are simple,” says Rakesh PS, who worked as a World Health Organization consultant supporting India’s National TB Elimination Program in Lakshadweep and parts of Kerala. “But simplicity of an idea should never be confused with ease of execution.”

India recorded about 2.7 million cases of tuberculosis in 2025, as ISignal reported in March 2026. Based on population projections for that year, this translates to an incidence of about 185 cases per 100,000 population.

In an upcoming book, Echoes from the Atoll, Rakesh writes about the challenges and the lessons that Lakshadweep’s TB programme holds.

The data was released by the government while responding to a question about how many billionaires were there in the country. The Ministry of Finance said that there was no statutory definition of the term “billionaire” in the Income Tax Act.

After checking the records, however, the officer informed Rayyan that there was a problem: she could not be “mapped” to the electoral roll. item.title: In his new book, former CEC SY Quraishi recounts discovering a TRP scam while running Doordarshan
item.description: An excerpt from ‘India and I: A Hundred Memories, Not a Memoir’, by SY Quraishi.
item.content:encoded:
The Television Rating Point (TRP) scandal exposed by the Mumbai Police in 2020 may look like a contemporary media shock, but for me, it was an old story resurfacing. Nearly two decades earlier, as director general of Doordarshan (2002–03), I saw the same design at work, cloaked in technical jargon, protected by “expert” consensus, and treated as unquestionable science.

At the time, Doordarshan’s reach was overwhelming. Across all television homes, terrestrial, cable, and satellite, DD accounted for 35 of the top 50 programmes. DD National’s prime-time news commanded nearly 92% viewership. Yet the ratings narrative portrayed Doordarshan as marginal, with just 2–3% share. What was carefully left unsaid: this figure referred only to cable and satellite (C&S) homes.

That omission was central to the scam. Nearly 50% of television households depended entirely on terrestrial broadcasting, where Doordarshan was the only channel. But advertising decisions were based almost exclusively on C&S homes. By defining C&S as “the market”, the system made a large part of India invisible. This was an organised distortion with clear consequences. DD’s reach remained vast, but its revenue shrank.

item.title: What the Cockroach Janta Party protests reveal about Indian Muslim leadership
item.description: The response to movement exposes the cost of allowing legitimate caution to become a substitute for civic engagement.
item.content:encoded:
Earlier this fortnight, in The Milli Gazette, I argued that Indian Muslims should resist evaluating every emerging movement solely through the lens of immediate Muslim interests. Democracies are not defended only when our own rights are threatened. They are defended whenever citizens insist that power remain accountable.

Over the past several weeks, I have watched the Cockroach Janta Party movement grow. I have also watched the Muslim response – not only the response of ordinary Muslims, but that of people and institutions regarded as community leaders.

Generally speaking, in spontaneous moments, while individual Muslims participate with conviction and passion, some established Muslim organisations and community leaders remain hesitant. Some wait. Some criticise. Some identify shortcomings. Others search for hidden motives. A number of them simply remain silent.

This scepticism is not irrational. Decades of surveillance, selective prosecution, media demonisation, communal violence and state manipulation have cultivated understandable caution. Distrust is often manufactured through repeated experience.

Nor is suspicion toward the Cockroach Janata Party uniquely Muslim. It has been widespread across many political and ideological spaces outside the Bharatiya Janata Party ecosystem. item.title: How long do fruits and vegetables stay fresh?
item.description: Humidity, temperature, light and how long produce has been in storage can all have an affect.
item.content:encoded:
Whether it’s trimming off a piece of mushy parsnip or cutting away a slightly mouldy bit of apple, many of us have used produce long after their peak of freshness.

While fruits and veggies are important for our health, they’re also highly susceptible to bacteria, fungi and other pathogenic microbes. Overripe fruit and veg can harbour E coli, Salmonella and Listeria bacteria, all of which can cause food poisoning. Understanding how to properly store fresh produce can maximise their freshness and keep them safe to eat for longer.

The use-by dates printed on packaging are usually a useful indicator of how long fresh produce can safely be stored and eaten. But the environment fresh produce is stored in can affect the shelf-life of produce – so use-by dates may not always be accurate.

Fruit and veg are living – so things like humidity, temperature, atmospheric gas, light, how long it’s been in storage and any potential microbial contamination can all affect how long produce can be stored.

The ideal storage conditions will also be different for each fruit and vegetable.

Apples have a shelf-life of around one week at room temperature, and three to four weeks in the fridge. These should ideally be stored in the fridge’s veg drawer and washed before eating.

item.title: ‘To mark my home within the luminescence of poetry’: Poems from a new book on the self in the city
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Absurd Theatre’, by Suchita Parikh-Mundul.
item.content:encoded:
To own a home

To own a home is to ingest it
and hope the concrete doesn’t
reverse track. It is to pray
the apartment breaks
down into paste in the entrails —
a process that takes as long
as final possession. It is to serve
the carpet area with a side of dadi’s
pickle (which the broker enjoys)
while the builder consumes seventy per cent
in cash, deep fried, and the rest
via bank transfer. (No salad.)

It is to feel lime-washed walls
slide down the throat with deceptive
sweetness and swirl in the abdomen
along with years of EMIs.
It is to brace for the acidity
of loan interests, corrosion of the inner
lining, lacerations and leakage.

It is to tackle complaints from neighbours,
which involves too much caffeine.
It is to watch the ceiling
peel, which is nobody’s concern
but yours. It is to devour meals
on the sly like a sleep-eater.
It is to decorate each room with care
and diabetic sugar, hoping everything
dissolves easily into bile. It is to feel
as if you have swallowed a rock,
though others are quick
to assure you this is normal
for property ownership and crucial
for a comfortable life.


Coastal road

The coastal road curves above the diamonds
of the Arabian Sea like an armful of edelweiss.
We drive towards its hologram
of urbanity, watching it expand like a promise,
noting how it links dreams to the soul.

The Union government on Monday introduced a bill to amend the anti-paper leak law in the wake of nationwide protests against alleged irregularities in competitive examinations.

The 2026 Public Examinations Prevention of Unfair Means Amendment Bill was introduced by Union minister Jitendra Singh as Opposition MPs shouted slogans criticising the police for using excessive force against protesters in Delhi on July 20.

Subsequently, the House was adjourned till 5 pm.

What does the bill say?

The legislation proposes imprisonment of five to ten years for individuals found using unfair means in public examinations. The maximum fine for such persons would increase from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 50 lakh.

If instances of paper leaks or other offences listed under the bill are found to be organised, the bill proposes a minimum sentence of seven years and a fine of up to Rs 10 crore.

A total of 15 illegal acts, including leaking question papers, tampering with optical mark recognition sheets, creating fake websites and issuing fake admit cards, have been listed as offences under the bill, reported The Indian Express.

item.title: This book asks if unemployment often translates to cynicism and desire for strong-armed leadership

India’s new slavery is an egregious version of this trend. item.title: India’s lost generation: Education was a secure investment, now it’s a gamble

A stark and urgent crisis has been unfolding in Indian society over the years. The dream of education as a guaranteed path to upward mobility has been crumbling. The “GenZ” protests we are witnessing in India today has brought the crisis into sharp relief but millions of families have long been suffering its consequences. Some of the aspects of the problem are still not fully acknowledged in public discourse.

item.title: Can you pay off your ‘sleep debt’?
item.description: Studying the effects of short sleep shows that biological systems are more dynamic and adaptable.
item.content:encoded:
Maybe you’re a new parent or someone who lies awake at night. If so, you may have started to worry you’re not getting enough sleep.

Sleep wearables don’t help. They can show your “sleep debt”, a running total of how far you’ve fallen behind.

But the word “debt” assumes your sleep works like a bank account. It assumes lost hours stack up, carry over, and you must eventually repay them in full.

But sleep doesn’t really work this way. And chasing “enough sleep” may not be helping.

What is a sleep debt?

Two systems control your sleep. One is your body clock, which helps keep wakefulness and sleep aligned with the day and night. The other is the one that matters here: sleep pressure.

Sleep pressure builds the longer you stay awake and eases while you sleep. At its highest, it’s hard to resist. Someone pulling an all-nighter might find themselves nodding off unintentionally.

This biological process is what “sleep debt” is trying to describe. If you sleep less than your body needs, pressure for sleep builds. Given the opportunity to recover after lost sleep, you sleep longer. In this broad sense, the debt metaphor works.

item.title: Greek-Roman philosopher Plutarch’s ancient advice for how to be happier online

For many centuries, the writings of Plutarch of Chaeronia (c.46-119CE) were at the heart of elite humanistic education in the West. We can see the influence of his Lives of Eminent Greeks and Romans and the philosophical essays in his work Moralia in early modern authors from Michel de Montaigne and Francis Bacon to William Shakespeare.

Many of Plutarch’s essays also have a practical focus that can seem very timely in our social media age. He writes about how to cool the desire to gossip and pry into other people’s lives and how not to be taken in by salacious stories.

He gives advice about how to avoid being triggered by others’ provocations and how to benefit from disagreement. He advises on how to speak about ourselves without boasting or self-advertisement, how to tell friends from conmen (or flatterers) trying to sell us something, and how to pay attention so our minds are not overloaded and scattered.

It almost seems as if Plutarch was peering into the 21st century and responding to the mental health challenges our commercialised social media is producing at scale.

The reality, as journalist Max Fisher outlines in his book The Chaos Machine, is that social media companies have identified the same psychological vulnerabilities Plutarch hoped to help readers to correct, recognising them as effective ways to “maximise user engagement”.

item.title: Does Britain’s political volatility reflect a broken democracy – compared to India’s stability?

Another change of guard in Downing Street has triggered a renewed bout of concern – and sniggers – over the fragility of British politics and its democracy. Not for the first time, as the country gets its seventh prime minister in 10 years. In many ways, it is. Repeated leadership upheavals have caused persistent government dysfunction. It’s a sign of the growing transience of voters’ loyalties to parties, making politics inherently volatile. item.description: When chronically online youth took to the streets, they stripped the state’s harshest response of the fear it was meant to inspire.

The Cockroach Janta Party was born as an Instagram page on May 16, when Abhijeet Dipke asked unemployed young people of the country, who the Chief Justice of India had dubbed “cockroaches”, to come together.

Its mascot was an AI-generated cockroach in sunglasses.

From that moment on, tens of thousands of young people rallied behind what was, in essence, an AI-slop Instagram page, and joined protests across the country.

The movement intensified after activist Sonam Wangchuk was forcibly removed from Jantar Mantar on the 21st day of his hunger strike, and when the police cracked down on their march towards Parliament with lathi charges, tear gas and pellet guns.

The young protestors responded to the violence – with memes and irreverence.

This was not a movement trying to imitate the student politics of the 1990s. It spoke the language of the internet because that was where much of its constituency already lived.

And so began the meme offensive.

Subway Surfers or lathi charge?

Take the “Everybody knows that I'm a good girl, officer” trend. The audio comes from Playing Dangerous, an unreleased 2012 Lana Del Rey song in which she playfully insists on her innocence to a police officer. item.title: ‘The Last Free Naga’: Jim Wungramyao Kasom’s short stories recreate the North East of the 1990s

“The mist rising from the river cast a blanket over the valley in the morning. The grass drooped low with dew. Time here was static and yet fleeting. The colours, the light, the mist changed every so often. Each moment, as magical as only time could weave. Time existed only as day and night, there were no hours or minutes.” writes Jim Wungramyao Kasom. This echoes across the 12 stories of The Last Free Naga, where he does something very simple. He tells us stories about people, places, land, jungle, and rivers. Simple, yes, but far from ordinary. The simplicity is deceptive. Kasom resists the usual push of romanticising his experience and stories and preserves and protects them with urgency, and in tune with their elemental rhythms.

item.title: How Mughal emperors embraced a syncretic sartorial sensibility
item.description: From self-expression to diplomatic posturing, Indic dress codes and textiles permeated their clothing choices.
item.content:encoded:
In his memoirs, the Tuzuk-i Jahangiri, Jahangir is represented as the quintessential aesthete. This is exemplified in his miniature portraits, often featuring a host of luxurious objects, such as jade wine cups, jewel-encrusted daggers, and finely woven textiles.

In one such painting, where he is depicted in his typical resplendent regalia, two overlapping textile sashes or patkas gracefully wind around his torso – one bearing a distinctive bandhani tie-dye design, emblematic of Rajputana culture, and the other displaying intricate Islamicate geometric designs.

These twin sashes depict a carefully crafted visual manifesto of the emperor’s filial identity – as the son of both his Muslim father, the Mughal emperor Akbar, and Hindu mother, Rajput princess Harkha Bai.

This kind of multicultural sartorial sensibility reached refined heights during the reign of Akbar and his successors but did not originate in Mughal courts. Art historian Finbarr Barry Flood in his book Objects of Translation argues that between the 10th and 12th centuries, medieval elites engaged in “cultural cross-dressing” at cosmopolitan zones of contact around mercantile hubs in northern India.

Muslim elites adopted luxury items of ornamentation and dress favoured by rich Hindu and Buddhist rulers while Buddhist and Hindu elites reciprocally took to “fashionable” Turko-Persian wear as a sign of their sophisticated, worldly tastes. Such exchanges...

item.title: ‘A Critical History of Kannada Literature’: A much-needed history of a major literary culture
item.description: Author Rajendra Chenni offers a critical history of Kannada literature, tracing its development from ancient texts to contemporary writing.
item.content:encoded:
Rajendra Chenni’s A Critical History of Kannada Literature is a timely, much-needed, readable history of one of India’s major literary cultures. While there have been such overviews before, it is necessary that each generation rewrite history with new foci and commitments. It is increasingly rare – in the age of academic specialisations – for scholars to be able to summon up a millennium and a half of literary production and be able to engage in good-faith conversation and dialogue with that tradition.

Chenni begins with some of the unavoidable issues of literary historiography. The first canonical text, the 9th-century Kavirajamarga, is celebrated as arguably the “first book of aesthetics in a vernacular language anywhere in the world”. Unsurprisingly, however, the content is deeply indebted to the Sanskrit tradition of scholars such as Bhamaha and Dandin.

The beginnings

What one thus needs is an appreciation of more reflective, rather than reflexive, nationalisms and sub-nationalisms. Further, the Kavirajamarga has a seemingly unproblematic engagement with worldly authority – it pits itself against other regional polities, but does not question aesthetics itself as needing to be homogenised and entirely aligned with political power.

item.title: Why you keep buying books you don’t read – and why it feels so good
item.description: Looking forward to enjoyable experiences, such as reading a new book, can improve mood, increase motivation and provide a buffer against everyday stress.
item.content:encoded:
At busy times, I find I simply cannot read as much as I would like to. Life has a habit of filling every available hour with work, meetings, emails, chores, errands and deadlines. Standing in one of my natural habitats – a bookshop – it is frustrating to see so many things I want to read while knowing I do not have the time.

My usual consolation is to buy the book anyway and let a small, satisfying pile build up, looking ahead to the next quieter stretch when I might finally open them. It is oddly satisfying. Some might call this clutter. The Japanese have a far more elegant word for it: tsundoku.

The term describes the habit of acquiring books and allowing them to accumulate unread. It combines the idea of stacking things up (tsunde), leaving something for later (oku) and reading (doku). The result is a concept that captures the quiet optimism of a pile of books.

Far from being a sign of being time poor or lacking in discipline, tsundoku may reveal something surprisingly important about how the brain responds to anticipation.

Every year, the foreign ministers of the 11 countries in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) get together to talk regional business.

These meetings tend to attract some big names from outside the region, too. At this year’s meeting this week in Manila, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will all attend.

Each power has its own reason to be there. The US wants to stay visible in a region that China has been courting. China wants to reassure its neighbours who are worried about its behaviour in the South China Sea, where run-ins with Philippine boats are now almost routine. And Russia wants to show it still has a seat at the table in the Asia-Pacific as its war in Ukraine grinds on.
